filled_passage:
I managed the sound at our class welcome evening. The computer held soft piano music, an end bell and a rooster call from our last play. I checked the music once, felt confident, then went to arrange chairs.

When guests entered, I pressed what I thought was the music button. A loud rooster cried out. Everyone turned towards me. I wished I could disappear.

Our teacher asked the class to wait. "Our guest from the farm has arrived unexpectedly," she said. The parents laughed. I took a breath and found the piano file.

The evening continued, but I kept thinking about my mistake. At the break, I told the teacher I should never touch the computer again.

"One wrong click doesn't mean you can't learn," she said. "What could help next time?"

The file names were nearly identical: sound1, sound2 and sound3. Another pupil had added a song, changing their order. I had remembered a position, not read a name.

We renamed them by their contents: Piano Welcome, End Bell and Rooster. I also listed when each was needed. Before the next part, I read both the name and the list instead of trusting my memory.

The class wanted to keep the rooster for future plays. We moved it into a different folder to avoid confusion.

Afterwards, a little brother asked to hear it again. I explained what I would play and pressed the button deliberately. This time, everyone knew what was coming.

While clearing up, I thanked the teacher for not making a small accident feel like a disaster. I recorded our solution to improve the setup for future users.

A month later, another pupil found the files easily with my notes. There was no surprise rooster. I still checked, though. Confidence didn't mean being certain I could never make an error. The old rooster was waiting for a play where it would be expected.
